name: Daslang (daScript)
baseline: Lua 5.5.1 and QuickJS 2026-06-04 (the same table also has LuaJIT 2.1 with -joff, Luau 0.736, Quirrel 4.29.1, Mono --interpreter)
workload: 16 kernels (sha256, dictionary, n-bodies, spectral norm, mandelbrot, exp loop, string2float, particles kinematics, queen, interop host calls, primes loop, tree, sort, fibonacci loop, float2string, fibonacci recursive); each cell is the median of five samples, each sample runs the kernel as often as fits a 0.5 s budget; interpreter lane compared with the Lua and QuickJS interpreters
claimed_speedup: On the Linux Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE interpreted table the DAS interpreter beats Lua and QuickJS on all 16 kernels: sha256 0.002510s vs Lua 0.068548s vs QuickJS 0.021312s; mandelbrot 0.001791s vs 0.056917s vs 0.006346s; sort 0.015450s vs 0.045629s vs 0.037570s; dictionary 0.011193s vs 0.038771s vs 0.047221s; tree 0.023617s vs 0.031137s vs 0.061180s; fibonacci recursive 0.048174s vs 0.048747s vs 0.088087s (about parity with Lua). Same pattern on Apple M1 Max (sha256 0.002792s vs Lua 0.068824s vs QuickJS 0.023714s). Ratios such as 27x vs Lua on sha256 and 8.5x vs QuickJS are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 19.1.7 on Linux, AppleClang 21.0.0.21000101 on macOS; daslang 0.6.4, LLVM 22.1.5; CMake default Release (-O3 per the CMakeLists comment); Lua 5.5.1 and QuickJS 2026-06-04 are built from pinned source tarballs by the same CMake project, their individual optimisation flags are not stated in the README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE w/ Radeon 780M Graphics (Linux) and Apple M1 Max (macOS)
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars (GaijinEntertainment/daScript); 0 stars on the benchmark repo borisbat/dasProfile
tradeoffs: Statically typed language with its own syntax (not drop-in for Lua or JavaScript code); zero-copy C++ interop by design; three execution tiers (interpreter, AOT to C++, LLVM JIT); interpreter startup is slower than Lua/QuickJS (hello world 0.0187s macOS / 0.0261s Linux vs about 0.0024-0.0039s for Lua and QuickJS).
caveats: The benchmark repo is written and maintained by the daslang developer (commits on the daScript repo are by the same account), so this is a first-party suite although it is fully public and reproducible; dasProfile itself shows no licence in the page opened (the language repo is BSD-3-Clause). LuaJIT -joff beats the DAS interpreter on 'tree' and 'fibonacci recursive' on Linux and Lua is within 1% on Linux fibonacci recursive. A separate third-party suite (sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, Windows, Visual Studio 17 2022, April 2026, code generated with Codex, CPU not stated) reports Daslang fastest on 13 of 16 workloads against Lua and AngelScript (fibonacci_recursive 266.421 vs Lua 599.702) but Lua wins sort (6.175 vs 237.142 ms) and string2float (68.624 vs 107.174 ms); the two suites use different kernel code, so the sort result is not directly comparable with the dasProfile row where DAS wins.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'script language shootout benchmark Lua Squirrel AngelScript Gravity Wren ChaiScript fibonacci github' surfaced sashi0034/script-language-benchmark, then 'daslang daScript benchmark vs Lua LuaJIT' surfaced borisbat/dasProfile

name: Escargot
baseline: QuickJS (Bellard release 2026-06-04); the same dashboard also runs V8 d8 and V8 --jitless
workload: SunSpider (26 scripts), Octane (18 benchmark functions) and Web Tooling Benchmark (18 functions) run in each engine's shell on one pinned CPU core of an ARM64 host; execution scores and fixed-work memory (RSS from smaps_rollup, median of 3 fresh processes) measured separately
claimed_speedup: ARM64 dashboard measured 2026-10-04 (Escargot fc608b59b): SunSpider 823.2 ms vs QuickJS 981.6 ms; Octane 2,198 vs 1,689; Web Tooling 1.07 vs 0.89 runs/s. Fixed-work memory average / peak RSS: Octane 85.7 / 157.4 MiB vs QuickJS 161.4 / 226.5; Web Tooling 171.6 / 212.7 vs 375.9 / 546.1; SunSpider 14.2 / 23.6 vs 5.3 / 9.0 (QuickJS lower). Ratios of about 1.19x (SunSpider), 1.30x (Octane) and 1.20x (Web Tooling) are derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: Escargot built as 'monthly-engine-release-arm64' (release build; exact compiler and flags not stated in the JSON); QuickJS taken from the official quickjs-2026-06-04.tar.xz and run as 'qjs --std --stack-size 8388608' (its build flags are not stated); glibc 2.39 runtime for all engines
hardware: aarch64 Linux 6.8.0-1063-aws, Arm CPU part 0xd0c (a Neoverse-N1-class core, inferred from the CPU part id), one core pinned for the engine and another for the monitor
stars_or_usage: 364 stars; 'used in shipping products' (Samsung, per README)
tradeoffs: Bytecode interpreter with no JIT and no executable memory needed; targets ECMAScript 2026 with ICU-backed Intl and Temporal (ICU dependency or bundle adds size); C++ embedding API plus optional Node-API layer; LGPL-2.1 licence.
caveats: First-party dashboard published by the Escargot project from its own CI runner (the harness and raw JSON are public, but the compiler and QuickJS build flags are not), so capped at tier C. QuickJS uses less memory than Escargot on SunSpider (5.3 vs 14.2 MiB average RSS), so the memory advantage only holds on the larger Octane and Web Tooling workloads. The score gains over QuickJS are 20-30%, not an order of magnitude. A prebuilt ARM32 dashboard exists too but was not opened. The pretty dashboard on samsung.github.io was not reachable; numbers were read from the gh-pages branch files latest.svg and latest.json.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): Samsung/escargot README 'Measured performance and memory' section (checked as a small-engine candidate while harvesting the JS engine shootouts); numbers read from the gh-pages branch files of the same repo

name: SpiderMonkey
workload: Score is the sum over the v8-v7 benchmark suite (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, NavierStokes), higher is better; run on GitHub Actions runners (ubuntu, macos-arm64, windows) and published in the repo README (snapshot 10/5/2026, 4:04:34 AM)
claimed_speedup: Score (higher is better), ubuntu / macos-arm64 / windows: spidermonkey 147.0 19137 / 25455 / 19049 vs quickjs 1217 / 1761 / 1067 vs duktape 489 / 905 / 371. About 15.7x QuickJS and 39x Duktape on ubuntu (derived from page data). Score per MB of binary is lower than the small interpreters (468/M vs quickjs 1190/M and duktape 1352/M on ubuntu).
hardware: GitHub Actions runners (ubuntu, macos-arm64, windows); CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 13.4k stars (mozilla-firefox/firefox, which contains js/src); used in Firefox
tradeoffs: Full optimising JIT engine with a C++ embedding API (JSAPI, mozilla-spidermonkey/spidermonkey-embedding-examples); heavy: 40.8M executable on ubuntu and 134.9M total on macOS vs 1M for QuickJS; long build; not a drop-in lightweight replacement for Duktape/QuickJS on small devices.
caveats: Engines are prebuilt through the suite owner's own *-build repos or taken as release binaries; compiler flags and CPU model are not stated (GitHub Actions runners), so this is a well-known third-party suite but short of tier A; the score is one v8-v7 aggregate (an older, partly micro-benchmark suite), engines are run as shells so startup and runtime wrappers can matter; SpiderMonkey runs with its JIT while QuickJS and Duktape are interpreters, so this measures a different class of engine; footprint and startup are far larger. The repo URL is the Firefox monorepo because SpiderMonkey source lives under js/src; the suite lists version 147.0 and builds it through the suite owner's ahaoboy/spidermonkey-build repo (its meson.build is derived from spidermonkey-embedding-examples and carries the label esr115), so the exact SpiderMonkey revision and build flags were not confirmed.
